## 5.1 Architecture

For each of Categories 1–7, annual tokens = global base (workers, seats, or transaction volume, in millions) × annual AI tasks per unit × tokens per task × penetration. Penetration is throughout an *effective*, intensity-normalized rate rather than a binary adoption count, but it denotes two different things depending on how the base is built. For the workforce-based categories it is the share of the base operating at the category's reference task frequency and token intensity; Section 4.1 develops that distinction explicitly for the category where the gap between an effective and an adoption reading is widest. For the volume-based Categories 3 and 5 it is the share of addressable items or interactions processed agentically at the reference token intensity. The workforce bases are built on an installed-base rather than a demographic method, but by two different routes. The non-coding workforce categories (2, 4, 6 and 7) are anchored to Microsoft 365's \~450 million commercial paid seats and partitioned with US BLS occupational ratios, so populations without a paid seat are excluded by construction. Category 1 is anchored differently: its 40 million is taken from published global developer-population estimates for the reasons set out in Section 4.1, with GitHub's \~150 million registrations serving only as an outer-TAM check and no occupational partition applied. Categories 3 and 5 are volume-based and use neither route. The full derivation, with a confidence grade on every input, is in the Base Sizing sheet of the companion workbook. The grades run A to D on a single axis — how directly the figure is observed: A, a directly observed or audited input (a disclosed seat count, a single-occupation actual); B, a whole occupational major group or an explicit published concept; C, a structured judgment or arbitrary split where no published basis exists; D, a forecast judgment. Source quality and allocation judgment are graded on the same scale, so an auditable seat count partitioned by a grade-C ratio yields a grade-C base. The model is intentionally free of prefill/decode decomposition, cache adjustment, and intra-year dynamics: it is an order-of-magnitude instrument whose every input is exposed for revision. A per-category compute weight (frontier = 1.0) converts nominal tokens into frontier-equivalent tokens — the series the companion infrastructure volume takes as its demand input.

## 5.2 Assumption anchors

Each coefficient is disciplined against an external anchor documented in the model workbook: the OpenRouter finding that programming exceeded half of routed tokens as of the platform's late-2025 usage study (Category 1's dominance); the Economic Index's doubling of sales-automation and trading-operations workflows (Categories 3–4 momentum) and its wage-to-Opus gradient (the compute weights); Sierra's disclosed call volumes (Category 5); published deep-research quotas — 25 queries per month on OpenAI's Plus, Team, Enterprise, and Edu plans and 250 on Pro — as the upper bound beneath which Category 6's 150-runs-per-year frequency is set; the per-developer intensity distribution from the companion report (Category 1's reference intensity of 750M tokens per developer-year sits in the upper-middle of the observed distribution, appropriate for a pool defined to exclude light users); the installed-base anchors for the non-coding workforce categories (Microsoft 365's \~450 million commercial seats scaled by US BLS occupational ratios, documented line by line in the Base Sizing sheet) and the published developer-population estimates behind Category 1's base; and — as validation only, never as a basis for adjusting any coefficient — a set of external reference points against which the total is checked for plausibility. Our 2026 total of \~20,100 trillion tokens per year (\~1,680 trillion per month) compares to OpenRouter alone at a reported \~100 trillion per month; to Google's disclosed throughput of more than 3,200 trillion tokens per month as of May 2026 (a seven-fold rise year-over-year, spanning consumer, Search, and internal surfaces), within which Google's model APIs alone run at roughly 19 billion tokens per minute, on the order of 830 trillion per month; and to the token volume implied by Anthropic's disclosed run-rate revenue, roughly 80% of which is business revenue, which at plausible blended prices for cache-heavy agentic traffic corresponds to several hundred trillion tokens per month from one vendor. A B2B-only, all-provider, seven-function estimate of \~1,680 trillion per month sits inside that corridor. The check runs in one direction. It can establish that the bottom-up total is of the right order; it cannot set any input, and by construction does not. Every figure in Table 2 is the product of the category-level coefficients in Section 4.

*Category rows are rounded independently; totals are computed on unrounded model output and may therefore differ from the sum of the displayed rows by one unit.*

Four readings of the table. First, coding's dominance remains decisive but no longer near-total: it holds 82% of nominal tokens in 2026 and 57% in 2028 — and, because it carries a 0.70 weight against the budget-model categories' 0.10–0.25, a still-larger share of compute-weighted demand, roughly 84% in 2026 easing to 64% by 2028. The table's most important feature is the shape of that decline. Coding's 2026 base is the product of the steepest acceleration the category will see; its year-over-year growth then falls to 1.18x and 1.11x, so that of the roughly 17,900 trillion tokens the seven functions add between 2026 and 2028, coding contributes 5,100 trillion and the six post-coding functions 12,800 trillion. Coding remains the largest workload throughout; from 2027 it is no longer the growth engine. Second, the growth column tracks the verification framework, with one instructive exception. The functions released from serial human review — reconciliation, verified by arithmetic; sales research and customer interaction, verified statistically by outcomes; and above all quantitative analysis, verified by execution — grow four- to ten-fold. The function whose verifier is a human reading grows 2.9x, and the function that had already saturated its verifier grows 1.3x. The exception is workflow automation, which grows eight-fold despite having no verifier at the moment of action: its expansion is catch-up from a 3% base as the semantic layer and control plane it depends on are built, not a graduation to autonomy, and its 24% endpoint remains among the lowest in the model — the verification constraint shows up in the level it reaches, not in the rate at which it closes the gap. That ordering emerges from the category-level assumptions rather than being imposed as an explicit growth-rate constraint, and it functions as an internal consistency check on the framework of Section 3 rather than as independent evidence for it — the penetration paths are themselves placed on the verification axis, as Section 6 states. Third, by absolute 2028 token contribution the post-coding order is Quantitative Analysis & Data Science (8,411T) \> Business Workflow Integration (3,240T) \> Qualitative Research (3,024T) — the last two nearly tied in nominal terms but far apart on a compute-weighted basis (2,419T weighted for Qualitative Research against 810T for Workflow Integration), a within-table illustration of the token-versus-compute principle: the connector workload emits more tokens, the judgment workload consumes more compute. Quantitative Analysis leads the post-coding field on both bases throughout, by a widening margin. Fourth, under the assumed weights the weighted total runs 32–38% below the nominal total — the quantitative expression, within this model, of the principle that token statistics read naively overstate infrastructure demand; the margin is a scenario output of the weight assumptions, not a measured error band. The divergence widens over the forecast precisely because the fastest-growing categories carry the lightest weights: Categories 3–5 and 7 together reach 13% of nominal tokens by 2028 while contributing under 5% of compute-weighted demand, and Category 6 does the reverse. The frontier-equivalent series in the table's final row, not the nominal total above it, is the figure the companion infrastructure volume converts into hardware requirements.
